messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 39

**Vignette: Mira, Age 37**

Mira grew up in the Philippines and has spent the better part of her adult life doing work she believes in — coordinating shelter placements and legal referrals for displaced families through an international aid organization based in the city where she now lives with her husband. She is the kind of person colleagues describe as steady, someone who has sat with people in the worst moments of their lives and managed to hold the space without flinching. That steadiness, she says, is something she no longer fully trusts in herself.

Two years ago, Mira was present at a protest near a detention facility where several of her clients were being held. The demonstration was peaceful, and she was there in a support capacity, documenting conditions and connecting families with legal observers. What happened next unfolded in less than four minutes, though she has since replayed it in fragments so many times that it feels both eternal and strangely incomplete. Police moved into the crowd without warning. She was shoved to the ground, and before she could orient herself, an officer struck her across the shoulders with a baton and pressed a knee into her back while she lay face-down on the pavement. She remembers the texture of the asphalt against her cheek, a woman nearby screaming, and the absolute certainty that she was going to be seriously hurt or killed. She was detained for several hours before being released without charges.

In the weeks that followed, Mira told herself she was fine. She had witnessed violence before — in the field, in the accounts of the families she served. She returned to work quickly, perhaps too quickly. But she began noticing things she couldn't explain away. She would drive past a police cruiser parked on the street and feel her chest seize, her hands going cold on the steering wheel. At intake appointments with new clients who had experienced state violence, she found herself dissociating mid-session, losing the thread of what was being said while some distant part of her was still pressed against that pavement. She started arriving late to meetings she used to lead with confidence, sitting closer to exits, scanning rooms in ways she recognized from the trauma histories she had spent years documenting in others.

Sleep has become its own ordeal. She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, sometimes certain she can still feel the weight on her back. Her husband, Marco, reaches for her and she lets him, but she has noticed herself pulling away during the day — shorter with him, less willing to be touched, as though her skin has become a site of vigilance rather than comfort. She has not told him the full shape of what she carries, partly because she worries it will frighten him and partly because she isn't sure she has the words for it yet.

What troubles Mira most is what has happened to her work. She still shows up. She still files the reports and makes the calls and sits across from families who have survived things she can barely imagine. But something has shifted in how she holds it. She finds herself avoiding cases that involve police contact, rerouting referrals in ways she knows are not always in her clients' best interest. There is a low-grade shame attached to this that she carries quietly, a sense that she has been compromised in the exact place she was supposed to be uncompromising. She has always understood, intellectually, that aid workers are not immune to the conditions they work within. She is now understanding it in a different register entirely.

She describes herself as someone who is still functioning, still present, still doing the work — but doing it, she says, "from behind glass." The world she moves through looks the same as it did before that afternoon. She just can't quite reach it the way she used to.
